warmup.text: In Chapter 26, Leader reaches Isaac's family, still hunting for Naomi. Ruth answers him without arguing at all. Today you will reread one passage and sum it up in two sentences: what happened, and what it meant.

words.text: Put the speaking roots to work today. Then learn how transition words, like but, because and instead, show how ideas connect. Then check your own draft, one spelling pattern at a time.

reading.text: Read Chapter 26 in your book. Watch what Ruth does when Leader demands her little girl, and what stops Pointy Nose. Then try the Read Like a Writer sentence that begins with Instead, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 26. Then revise your draft with the checklist: strong verbs, a combined sentence, clear pronouns, and at least one transition word. Star your three best sentences.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Join the second one into one clear sentence, out loud.
Tap Check My Work.
how.why: Joining short sentences shows the reader how the ideas connect.

do: Read each meaning.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
Match all four words.
how.why: If you know the root, you can work out a word you have never seen.

do: Type the word that fits each sentence.
Open the Word Bank if you need it.
Tap Check My Words.
how.why: Putting a word back in its sentence shows you really know it.

do: Read the Transitions box.
Tap the better combination in each pair.
Revise a paragraph of your own in the box, with one transition word.
how.why: Transition words tell the reader how one idea connects to the next.

do: Ask: is the base a whole word?
Is it a person who does something?
Tap a word, then tap its column.
how.why: These are the spellings students most often miss in a final draft.

do: Tap your lens for today.
Reread one passage from Chapter 26.
Sum it up in two sentences: what happened, and what it meant.
how.why: A short summary only works if it would not mislead someone who has not read it.
how.use: You will use this in the Read Like a Writer box.

do: Read Chapter 26 first.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
For question 3, use one detail from each chapter.
how.why: These questions check what happened and what the author shows you.

do: Read your draft from Day 2.
Check it against the list, one pass at a time.
Star your three best sentences and rewrite one.
how.why: Revising means making the piece clearer, not starting over.
how.use: Next lesson you will write the final version.

do: Read what justice means.
Read the example from this week.
After you read, use the justice meter at the end of this tab.
Read the chapter introduction below.
Open your book and read Chapter 26.
Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch below.

glossary.meaning: a word that shows how one idea connects to the next

exhausted: Joseph had a very long day.
revenge: Leader wants this in the morning.

miss.dependable: depend is a whole word, so it takes -able.
miss.possible: poss is not a word by itself, so it takes -ible.
miss.printer: a person or machine that prints: -er.
miss.remarkable: remark is a whole word, so it takes -able.
miss.terrible: terr is not a word by itself, so it takes -ible.
miss.visible: vis is not a word by itself, so it takes -ible.

game.title: Raise Your Voice
game.sub: This week's word game · 3 lines today
game.look: Each line is something a person in Isaac's time could say. These lines are made up; they are not from the book. Read the whole line, then tap the word that fits the blank. Each line you finish sends a gold voice ring into the sky.

do: Read the whole line, blank and all.
Ask: voice and calling, or saying?
Tap the word that fits.
Tap Next line.
how.why: If you know voc, voke and dict, you can work out words you have never studied.

game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for three more lines.

lines.before: I will read the sentences slowly, and you write them down. This is called
lines.why: dict (say) + ation: words said out loud for someone to write.

lines.after: this winter. Snow one day, rain the next.
lines.why: un (not) + pre (before) + dict (say) + able: no one can say ahead of time.

lines.before: Hum first. Then open your mouth and
lines.why: voc (voice) + al + ize: to make a sound with your voice.

art.title: The Rattle-Snake
art.alt: A hand-colored drawing of a coiled brown and black rattlesnake with its head raised and its rattle in the air.
art.look: Mark Catesby drew and colored this timber rattlesnake for a book about the animals and plants of Carolina and Florida, printed in London in 1743. The small words are Latin labels: Vipera caudisona means the viper with a sounding tail. In Chapter 26, a rattlesnake rises over Nita.

virtue.name: justice
virtue.title: The justice meter
virtue.intro: Think about one moment from Chapter 26.
virtue.moment: Leader demands Ruth's little girl. Ruth does not argue. She carries Nita's body, wrapped in a blanket, lays it by the fire, and says, “Here is my daughter.”
virtue.ask: How much justice did Ruth show? Slide to show.
virtue.take: Mason's take: a lot. She told the truth calmly, and the soldiers had to see what had happened.
